concepts.def: A system in which both energy and matter can enter and exit. Ecosystems are open systems: light energy enters and heat leaves, while matter such as water, carbon dioxide, mineral ions and migrating organisms also passes across the boundary in both directions.

A system in which energy can pass in and out but matter cannot. A sealed glass bottle garden is an approximately closed system: light enters and heat escapes, but no atoms enter or leave, so all the matter inside must be recycled.
A community of organisms together with the abiotic environment with which they interact. Because energy and matter both cross its boundary, an ecosystem is treated as an open system.

Light energy from the Sun, captured by photosynthesis in producers, is the source of almost all the energy that flows through ecosystems. The exceptions are ecosystems in oceans below the depth of light penetration and in some caves, where chemoautotrophs supply the energy.

Communities around deep-sea hydrothermal vents, below the level of light penetration, and in some caves sealed from outside organic matter, in which the energy entering the food chains comes from chemoautotrophic bacteria oxidizing inorganic substances rather than from photosynthesis.

A generalized principle, or rule of thumb, formulated to describe a pattern observed in nature. Unlike a theory, a law does not offer an explanation for the pattern, but like a theory it can be used to make predictions. A useful generalization describes many observations concisely, holds in the great majority of cases and allows testable predictions to be made.
A sequence of organisms in which each is a food source for the next. Chemical energy in carbon compounds passes to a consumer as it feeds on the organism that is the previous stage in the chain.

The one-way passage of energy along a food chain, stored in the carbon compounds of the organism being eaten. The energy is transferred by feeding, is released by cell respiration in each organism and is ultimately lost from the ecosystem as heat; it is not recycled.

A diagram made up of all the interconnected food chains in a community, showing the feeding relationships between its organisms. It is best constructed from a local community that students have observed.
In a food chain or food web an arrow points from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it, indicating the direction of transfer of energy and biomass.

A heterotroph, typically a fungus or bacterium, that obtains its energy and carbon from carbon compounds in dead organic matter, which it digests externally. Its energy supply is the organic matter coming from dead organisms: faeces, dead parts of organisms and dead whole organisms.

Carbon compounds in material that is no longer part of a living organism, including faeces, dead parts of organisms such as shed leaves and hair, and dead whole organisms. It is the energy source for decomposers and detritus feeders.

An organism that uses an external energy source to synthesize the carbon compounds it requires from simple inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide and water. Energy is needed both for carbon fixation and for the anabolic reactions that build macromolecules.

The conversion of inorganic carbon dioxide into organic carbon compounds by an autotroph. It is an energy-requiring process, and the energy comes from the autotroph's external energy source: light in photoautotrophs and oxidation reactions in chemoautotrophs.
Reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones, such as the synthesis of polysaccharides, proteins and nucleic acids from monomers. They require an input of energy, usually supplied by ATP.
An autotroph that uses light as its external energy source, converting light energy into chemical energy in carbon compounds by photosynthesis. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria are photoautotrophs.

An autotroph that uses energy released by oxidation reactions of inorganic substances as its external energy source for carbon fixation. Iron-oxidizing bacteria, which oxidize iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions, are an example.

concepts.term: Oxidation reaction as an energy source
concepts.def: A reaction in which a substance loses electrons. Oxidation reactions release energy, which is why they are useful to living organisms: chemoautotrophs use the energy from oxidizing inorganic substances such as iron(II) ions, and all organisms use the energy from oxidizing carbon compounds in cell respiration.

An organism that obtains carbon compounds from other organisms and uses them to synthesize the carbon compounds that it requires. Complex compounds such as proteins and nucleic acids are digested, externally or internally, and the products are then assimilated.

The breakdown of complex carbon compounds into smaller molecules that can be absorbed. In internal digestion the food is taken into the organism first, as in the gut of an animal; in external digestion enzymes are secreted onto the food and the products are absorbed, as in fungi and many bacteria.

The use by a heterotroph of the absorbed products of digestion, such as amino acids and monosaccharides, to construct the carbon compounds that it requires, so that they become part of its own biomass.

The controlled oxidation of carbon compounds inside cells to release energy, which is used to make ATP. It takes place in both autotrophs and heterotrophs, at all times, and is distinct from breathing and gas exchange.

The position of an organism in a food chain, defined by the number of feeding steps between it and the producer. Many organisms have a varied diet and so occupy different trophic levels in different food chains.

concepts.term: Producer, primary, secondary and tertiary consumer
concepts.def: The names of the successive trophic levels. A producer is an autotroph at the start of a food chain; a primary consumer feeds on producers; a secondary consumer feeds on primary consumers; a tertiary consumer feeds on secondary consumers.

A diagram of horizontal bars, one for each trophic level with producers at the base, whose widths are proportional to the energy flowing through that level, measured as energy per unit area per unit time (for example kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹). It is constructed from research data for a specific ecosystem and shows the energy losses between levels.

The reduction in energy available at each successive stage of a food chain. Causes include: not all of an organism is eaten; not all of what is eaten is digested and absorbed, some being egested in faeces; and much of the absorbed energy is released by cell respiration and lost as heat. Only energy stored in new biomass can pass to the next level.

A heterotroph such as an earthworm or woodlouse that ingests dead organic matter and digests it internally. Detritus feeders and decomposers are not usually shown in food chains, but they obtain the energy in uneaten material and faeces from every trophic level and release it as heat through cell respiration.

The conversion of chemical energy to heat in all organisms, autotrophs and heterotrophs alike. Energy transfers are not 100% efficient, so heat is produced both when ATP is made in cell respiration and when ATP is used in cells; this heat is lost to the environment and cannot be reused by organisms.

concepts.term: Restriction on the number of trophic levels
concepts.def: Because so much energy is lost at each transfer, the energy remaining after four or five stages is too small to support a further trophic level at a viable population size. At each successive stage there are fewer organisms or smaller organisms and therefore less biomass.

The total mass of organic matter in the organisms of a trophic level or ecosystem, usually measured as dry mass. Biomass falls at each successive trophic level, but the energy content per unit mass of biomass is not reduced.

The accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs, expressed as a rate: mass of carbon per unit area per unit time, usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹. Biomass accumulates when organisms grow or reproduce, and biomes differ greatly in their capacity to accumulate it.

A group of ecosystems with similar communities and climate, such as tropical rainforest, temperate grassland or desert. Biomes vary in their capacity to accumulate biomass because factors such as water availability, temperature and light limit primary production.

The accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by heterotrophs, measured in the same units as primary production. It is lower than primary production in an ecosystem because much of the carbon that heterotrophs consume is converted to carbon dioxide and water in cell respiration rather than being added to biomass.

The recycling of carbon within an ecosystem, shown in a diagram of pools and fluxes: photosynthesis moves carbon from atmospheric carbon dioxide into carbon compounds in producers; feeding moves carbon compounds from producers to consumers; cell respiration in all organisms returns carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

An ecosystem, or other reservoir, that takes up more carbon dioxide than it releases. An ecosystem is a sink when photosynthesis exceeds the total respiration of all its organisms, giving a net uptake of carbon dioxide.
An ecosystem, or other reservoir, that releases more carbon dioxide than it takes up. An ecosystem is a source when respiration exceeds photosynthesis, giving a net release of carbon dioxide.

The rapid oxidation of carbon compounds in the presence of oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and heat. Combustion of biomass, peat, coal, oil and natural gas returns to the atmosphere carbon that was fixed by photosynthesis, in some cases hundreds of millions of years ago.

Peat, coal, oil and natural gas: stores of carbon compounds derived from organisms that were not fully decomposed. They vary greatly in date of formation, from peat still forming today to coal, oil and gas formed over tens to hundreds of millions of years. Combustion after lightning strikes happens naturally, but human activities have greatly increased combustion rates.

The record of atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration measured continuously at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958. It shows a long-term rise, from about 315 ppm to over 420 ppm, superimposed on an annual fluctuation of a few parts per million.

The two features of the Keeling Curve. The annual fluctuation arises because Northern Hemisphere photosynthesis exceeds respiration in spring and summer, drawing carbon dioxide down, while respiration exceeds photosynthesis in autumn and winter. The long-term rising trend is due to combustion of fossil fuels and biomass adding carbon dioxide faster than ecosystems and oceans remove it.

The huge annual exchanges of gases between organisms and the atmosphere. Aerobic respiration depends on atmospheric oxygen produced by photosynthesis, and photosynthesis depends on atmospheric carbon dioxide produced by respiration, making this a major interaction between autotrophs and heterotrophs.

The repeated movement of every element required by living organisms, not just carbon, between organisms and the abiotic environment. Decomposers play a key role by breaking down dead organic matter and releasing elements in inorganic forms that autotrophs can take up again.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes an ecosystem as a system?
options: It is an open system: energy enters and leaves it and so does matter, such as water, gases and organisms.
It is a closed system: light energy enters and heat leaves, but all of its matter is recycled within it.
It is a closed system: neither energy nor matter can cross its boundary once the community is established.
It is an open system for matter only, because the energy in it is recycled from decomposers back to producers.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ecosystems are open: energy and matter both cross the boundary
mcqs.explain: Ecosystems are open systems in which both energy and matter can enter and exit. Light enters and heat leaves, and matter such as rainwater, carbon dioxide and migrating animals crosses the boundary in both directions.
rationales: Ecosystems are open systems in which both energy and matter can enter and exit. Light enters and heat leaves, and matter such as rainwater, carbon dioxide and migrating animals crosses the boundary in both directions.

A student who pictures an ecosystem as a self-contained unit recycling its own matter picks this. That describes a closed system; real ecosystems exchange water, gases, ions and organisms with their surroundings, so they are open.
A student who takes 'closed' to mean sealed against everything picks this. Even in a closed system energy passes in and out; only matter is confined. An ecosystem is not closed at all.

A student who believes energy is recycled like nutrients picks this. Energy flows through an ecosystem and leaves as heat; it must enter continuously, so an ecosystem is open to energy as well as matter.

mcqs.q: A glass bottle containing soil, moss and small plants was sealed in 1972 and left on a windowsill. The plants are still alive decades later. How should this bottle garden be classified as a system, and why?
options: Isolated, because nothing at all crosses the glass, so the plants survive on the energy that was sealed in with them.
Closed, because light energy enters through the glass and heat leaves, but no matter passes in or out.
Closed, because energy is recycled inside the bottle between plants and decomposers, so nothing needs to enter.
Closed, because light enters but no energy can leave, since plants do not release heat to their surroundings.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ecosystems are open: energy and matter both cross the boundary
mcqs.explain: In closed systems only energy is able to pass in and out. The sealed bottle admits light for photosynthesis and loses heat, while every atom of water, carbon and oxygen inside is recycled between the plants and the soil organisms.
rationales: A student who thinks a sealed container stops energy as well as matter picks this. Glass transmits light and conducts heat; without an energy input the plants would have died within months, since every energy transfer loses heat.

In closed systems only energy is able to pass in and out. The sealed bottle admits light for photosynthesis and loses heat, while every atom of water, carbon and oxygen inside is recycled between the plants and the soil organisms.

A student who believes energy cycles like matter picks this. Chemical energy is released as heat at every transfer and cannot be reused, so the system depends on light entering continuously; only matter is recycled.

A student who believes only warm-blooded animals produce heat picks this. Plants and soil microorganisms respire and convert chemical energy to heat, which leaves through the glass; if it did not, the bottle would heat up continuously.

mcqs.q: Dense communities of tube worms, clams and shrimps live around hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor, far below the depth to which light penetrates. What is the principal source of the energy that sustains these communities?
options: Dead organic matter produced by photosynthesis at the surface, sinking down to the vents from the sunlit water above.
Bacteria that photosynthesize using the faint light emitted by the hot, mineral-rich water leaving the vents.
Bacteria that fix carbon using energy released by oxidizing inorganic substances emerging from the vents.
Bacteria that respire dissolved carbon compounds carried up from below the sea floor in the hot vent water.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sunlight powers almost every ecosystem, and laws describe rather than explain
mcqs.explain: Sunlight sustains most ecosystems, but ecosystems below the level of light penetration in oceans are exceptions. Chemoautotrophic bacteria oxidize inorganic substances such as hydrogen sulfide from the vent fluid and use the energy to synthesize carbon compounds, forming the base of the food chains.
rationales: A student convinced that every ecosystem must trace back to sunlight picks this. A small amount of surface material does sink to the deep sea floor, but it is far too little to feed the dense vent communities, which are sustained by chemoautotrophs.
A student who assumes every autotroph must be photosynthetic picks this. The vent bacteria that support the community are chemoautotrophs; light is not their energy source.

Sunlight sustains most ecosystems, but ecosystems below the level of light penetration in oceans are exceptions. Chemoautotrophic bacteria oxidize inorganic substances such as hydrogen sulfide from the vent fluid and use the energy to synthesize carbon compounds, forming the base of the food chains.

A student who thinks 'oxidation as an energy source' must mean respiring organic matter picks this. The vent bacteria oxidize inorganic substances and fix carbon dioxide; they do not depend on a supply of ready-made carbon compounds.

mcqs.q: A rabbit eats grass and is later eaten by a fox. In what form does chemical energy pass from the rabbit to the fox?
options: In the carbon compounds of the rabbit's tissues, which the fox digests, absorbs and later oxidizes in cell respiration.
In the ATP stored in the rabbit's cells, which the fox absorbs intact and uses directly as its energy currency.
In the heat of the rabbit's body, which is transferred to the fox and then recycled back to the grass when the fox dies.
In the oxygen the fox breathes in while it eats, since it is oxygen rather than food that supplies the energy for its cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chemical energy passes along the chain by feeding
mcqs.explain: Chemical energy passes to a consumer as it feeds on an organism that is the previous stage in the food chain. The energy is held in the rabbit's carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and is released only when the fox's cells oxidize the products of digestion.
rationales: Chemical energy passes to a consumer as it feeds on an organism that is the previous stage in the food chain. The energy is held in the rabbit's carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and is released only when the fox's cells oxidize the products of digestion.

A student who thinks of ATP as the molecule that carries energy from one organism to another picks this. ATP is made and used inside each organism's own cells; the energy passed on in feeding is in carbon compounds.

A student who believes energy cycles round the ecosystem picks this. Heat cannot be used by organisms and is lost to the environment; the fox gains chemical energy, and no energy returns to the grass.

A student who equates respiration with breathing and thinks energy comes from oxygen picks this. Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, but the energy released comes from oxidizing the carbon compounds obtained in food.

mcqs.q: In a local hedgerow, caterpillars and aphids both feed on hawthorn leaves. Blue tits eat caterpillars, ladybirds eat aphids, and sparrowhawks eat blue tits. Which is a correctly constructed food chain from this community?
options: sparrowhawk → blue tit → caterpillar → hawthorn
hawthorn leaves → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk
hawthorn → caterpillar → aphid → ladybird → sparrowhawk
soil fungi → hawthorn → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk
mcqs.specStatementText: Drawing food chains and webs
mcqs.explain: Each arrow points from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it, indicating the direction of transfer of energy and biomass: hawthorn leaves feed caterpillars, which feed blue tits, which feed sparrowhawks.
rationales: A student who reads the arrow as 'eats' draws the chain from predator to prey. Arrows show the direction in which energy and biomass are transferred, so they must run from the hawthorn towards the sparrowhawk.

Each arrow points from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it, indicating the direction of transfer of energy and biomass: hawthorn leaves feed caterpillars, which feed blue tits, which feed sparrowhawks.

A student who joins any two organisms that interact, including competitors, picks this. Caterpillars and aphids both eat hawthorn but neither eats the other, so no arrow can connect them; nor was any feeding link from ladybirds to sparrowhawks described.
A student who thinks decomposers are producers that feed the plant picks this. The hawthorn does not eat fungi; it fixes its own carbon using light, so a food chain begins with the producer.

mcqs.q: What do the arrows in a food web represent?
options: The direction in which each consumer seeks its food, pointing from the feeder to the organism that it eats.
Every ecological interaction in the community, including competition between species that share a food source.
The direction in which energy and biomass are transferred, from each organism to the organism that feeds on it.
The route by which energy is returned from decomposers to producers so that it can pass around the community again.
mcqs.specStatementText: Drawing food chains and webs
mcqs.explain: Arrows in food chains and food webs indicate the direction of transfer of energy and biomass, so they run from the food organism to the consumer.
rationales: A student who reads the arrow as the verb 'eats' picks this. The convention is the reverse: the arrow follows the energy and biomass, from the eaten to the eater.
A student who treats a food web as a map of all relationships picks this. A food web shows feeding relationships only; competitors are not joined by arrows.
Arrows in food chains and food webs indicate the direction of transfer of energy and biomass, so they run from the food organism to the consumer.
A student who believes energy is recycled picks this. Arrows show one-way transfer of energy and biomass by feeding; energy leaves the community as heat and is not returned to producers.

mcqs.q: What is the source of energy for decomposers such as soil fungi and bacteria?
options: Simple inorganic substances in the soil, from which decomposers synthesize their own carbon compounds using energy from sunlight.
Dead whole organisms and dead parts of organisms only, because faeces are waste from which all of the energy has been removed.
The bodies of tertiary consumers only, because decomposers are the final link in a food chain and feed on the top level.
Carbon compounds in organic matter from dead organisms, including faeces, dead parts of organisms and dead whole organisms.
mcqs.specStatementText: Decomposers live on dead organic matter
mcqs.explain: Decomposers are heterotrophs whose energy supply is the carbon compounds in dead organic matter. Faeces, shed leaves and other dead parts, and whole dead organisms all contain carbon compounds that the decomposers digest externally and then oxidize in cell respiration.
rationales: A student who classes decomposers as producers picks this. Decomposers do not fix carbon; they obtain both carbon and energy from the organic matter of dead organisms.
A student who thinks 'waste' means energy-free picks this. Faeces contain undigested carbon compounds and are an important energy source for decomposers and detritus feeders.

A student who places decomposers as the last trophic level picks this. Decomposers receive dead matter and faeces from every trophic level, producers included, and are not usually shown as part of a food chain.

Decomposers are heterotrophs whose energy supply is the carbon compounds in dead organic matter. Faeces, shed leaves and other dead parts, and whole dead organisms all contain carbon compounds that the decomposers digest externally and then oxidize in cell respiration.

mcqs.q: A photoautotroph fixes carbon dioxide into carbon compounds and then uses these to build macromolecules such as starch and cellulose. Which statement about the energy involved is correct?
options: Both carbon fixation and the anabolic reactions that build macromolecules need energy, supplied ultimately by light.
The autotroph generates its own energy as it synthesizes the carbon compounds, so no external energy source is needed.
Energy is needed for carbon fixation, but the anabolic reactions run on light directly because photoautotrophs do not respire.
No energy is needed for either process, because the carbon compounds absorbed through the roots already contain the energy.
mcqs.specStatementText: Autotrophs build carbon compounds from inorganic ones, using outside energy
mcqs.explain: Autotrophs use an external energy source to synthesize carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances. Energy is required for carbon fixation and for the anabolic reactions that build macromolecules; in a photoautotroph that energy comes from light.
rationales: Autotrophs use an external energy source to synthesize carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances. Energy is required for carbon fixation and for the anabolic reactions that build macromolecules; in a photoautotroph that energy comes from light.

A student who hears 'makes its own food' as 'makes its own energy' picks this. Energy cannot be created; the autotroph converts light energy into chemical energy, and without the light supply neither fixation nor anabolism could proceed.

A student who thinks photosynthesis replaces respiration in plants picks this. Anabolic reactions are driven by ATP, and photoautotrophs make ATP by cell respiration as well as in photosynthesis; they respire continuously.

A student who believes plants take in carbon compounds from the soil picks this. Roots absorb water and mineral ions; the carbon comes from carbon dioxide, and fixing it into carbon compounds requires an input of energy.

mcqs.q: Iron-oxidizing bacteria live in mine drainage water in darkness. How do they obtain the energy they need to synthesize carbon compounds?
options: From photosynthesis, using pigments that can capture the very low levels of light reaching the mine drainage water.
From the oxidation of iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions, which releases energy that is used to fix carbon dioxide.
From cell respiration of carbon compounds that they absorb from the organic matter dissolved in the water.
They need no energy source, because autotrophs generate energy themselves while synthesizing carbon compounds.
mcqs.specStatementText: Light for photoautotrophs, oxidation reactions for chemoautotrophs
mcqs.explain: Oxidation reactions release energy, so they are useful in living organisms. Iron-oxidizing bacteria are chemoautotrophs: the energy from oxidizing iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions is the external energy source for their carbon fixation.
rationales: A student who assumes all autotrophs are photosynthetic picks this. These bacteria are chemoautotrophs; their energy source is an oxidation reaction, not light.

Oxidation reactions release energy, so they are useful in living organisms. Iron-oxidizing bacteria are chemoautotrophs: the energy from oxidizing iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions is the external energy source for their carbon fixation.

A student who thinks the only energy-yielding oxidation is respiration of organic matter picks this. Respiring absorbed carbon compounds would make the bacteria heterotrophs; iron-oxidizing bacteria oxidize an inorganic ion and fix their own carbon.
A student who believes autotrophs make energy picks this. Carbon fixation requires an input of energy from an external source; in these bacteria it is the oxidation of iron(II) ions.

mcqs.q: A bacterial culture was kept in complete darkness in a medium containing only dissolved iron(II) ions, carbon dioxide, oxygen and mineral salts, with no carbon compounds. Over several days the bacterial biomass increased and iron(III) accumulated. What is the best conclusion?
options: The culture must have been exposed to some light, because synthesizing carbon compounds from carbon dioxide requires light.
The bacteria respired carbon compounds present as contaminants, and the iron(III) formed by ordinary chemical rusting.
The bacteria are chemoautotrophs that used energy from oxidizing iron(II) to synthesize carbon compounds from carbon dioxide.
The bacteria generated the energy for growth themselves, so the oxidation of iron(II) was an unrelated side reaction.
mcqs.specStatementText: Light for photoautotrophs, oxidation reactions for chemoautotrophs
mcqs.explain: Biomass increased with no organic carbon available, so the bacteria must have fixed carbon dioxide. There was no light, so the energy source was not photosynthesis; the accumulation of iron(III) shows that iron(II) was oxidized, and oxidation reactions release the energy needed for carbon fixation.
rationales: A student who believes carbon fixation always depends on light picks this. Chemoautotrophs fix carbon in darkness using energy from oxidation reactions; the iron(III) that accumulated is the evidence of that oxidation.

A student who thinks bacteria can only gain energy by respiring organic matter picks this. The medium contained no carbon compounds, so the biomass gained must have been built from carbon dioxide, which needs an energy source: the iron oxidation.

Biomass increased with no organic carbon available, so the bacteria must have fixed carbon dioxide. There was no light, so the energy source was not photosynthesis; the accumulation of iron(III) shows that iron(II) was oxidized, and oxidation reactions release the energy needed for carbon fixation.
A student who believes autotrophs create their own energy picks this. Energy cannot be generated from nothing; the growth was powered by the energy released when iron(II) was oxidized to iron(III).

mcqs.q: A heterotroph eats food containing proteins. Which statement describes how it uses the carbon compounds in this food?
options: It absorbs the proteins intact through its gut wall and uses them directly, since a protein from food is already functional.
It can use the proteins only if it has a gut, because digestion of complex carbon compounds cannot take place outside a cell.
It oxidizes all of the proteins in cell respiration to release energy, since heterotrophs cannot synthesize proteins themselves.
It digests the proteins to amino acids, absorbs these and assimilates them by building the specific proteins that it needs.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heterotrophs digest, absorb and rebuild
mcqs.explain: Heterotrophs use carbon compounds obtained from other organisms to synthesize the carbon compounds that they require. Complex compounds such as proteins are digested, externally or internally, and the products are assimilated into the heterotroph's own molecules.
rationales: A student who thinks the protein eaten is the protein used picks this. Proteins are too large to be absorbed and would be the wrong proteins anyway; they are digested to amino acids and the heterotroph constructs its own.

A student who equates digestion with the gut picks this. Digestion can be external: fungi and many bacteria secrete enzymes onto food and absorb the products, then assimilate them just as an animal does.

A student who thinks food is either burned or stored, never rebuilt, picks this. Heterotrophs synthesize their own proteins from absorbed amino acids; only some of the carbon compounds in food are respired.

Heterotrophs use carbon compounds obtained from other organisms to synthesize the carbon compounds that they require. Complex compounds such as proteins are digested, externally or internally, and the products are assimilated into the heterotroph's own molecules.

mcqs.q: A bracket fungus grows on a dead tree trunk. How does it obtain the carbon compounds it requires from the wood?
options: It secretes enzymes onto the wood, absorbs the small molecules produced by this external digestion and assimilates them.
It takes fragments of wood into its cells and digests them internally, since digestion can only happen inside an organism.
It synthesizes its own carbon compounds from the mineral ions in the decaying wood, using the energy released by decay.
It absorbs the cellulose and other macromolecules of the wood intact through its cell walls and uses them unchanged.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heterotrophs digest, absorb and rebuild
mcqs.explain: Complex carbon compounds are digested either externally or internally. Fungi digest externally: enzymes released into the wood break down its carbon compounds, the products are absorbed, and the fungus then constructs the carbon compounds that it requires.
rationales: Complex carbon compounds are digested either externally or internally. Fungi digest externally: enzymes released into the wood break down its carbon compounds, the products are absorbed, and the fungus then constructs the carbon compounds that it requires.
A student who thinks digestion is always internal picks this. Fungal cells cannot ingest solid particles; they digest the wood outside their cells and absorb the products.
A student who classes decomposers as producers picks this. A fungus is a heterotroph: it cannot fix carbon and obtains both carbon and energy from the carbon compounds of the dead wood.
A student who thinks food macromolecules can be used as they are picks this. Cellulose and lignin are far too large to cross membranes; they must be digested to small molecules first.

mcqs.q: Which organisms release energy by the oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration?
options: Heterotrophs at all times, but autotrophs only at night, when they cannot obtain energy from photosynthesis.
All autotrophs and all heterotrophs, in every living cell, throughout the day and the night.
Only organisms with lungs or gills, because respiration depends on breathing to take in oxygen from the air or water.
Heterotrophs and chemoautotrophs only, because photoautotrophs use light rather than oxidation as their energy source.
mcqs.specStatementText: Every organism respires, all the time
mcqs.explain: Energy is released in both autotrophs and heterotrophs by oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration. Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals all respire continuously; photosynthesis in autotrophs is an additional process, not a replacement.
rationales: A student who sees photosynthesis and respiration as alternatives picks this. Autotrophs respire in the light as well; in daylight the net gas exchange is dominated by photosynthesis, but respiration has not stopped.

Energy is released in both autotrophs and heterotrophs by oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration. Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals all respire continuously; photosynthesis in autotrophs is an additional process, not a replacement.
A student who confuses cell respiration with breathing picks this. Cell respiration is a chemical process in cells; plants, fungi and bacteria respire without any breathing organs.

A student who thinks oxidation and light are alternative energy sources that exclude each other picks this. Light powers carbon fixation in photoautotrophs, but they still oxidize carbon compounds in cell respiration to release energy for their cells.

mcqs.q: In a garden, blackbirds eat berries from shrubs and also eat snails, which feed on the leaves of the same shrubs. Which trophic level or levels does the blackbird occupy?
options: A secondary consumer only, because each species has a single trophic level that is fixed by its usual diet.
Secondary consumer in both chains, because a bird that eats animals is a carnivore and carnivores are secondary consumers.
A primary consumer in the chain where it eats berries and a secondary consumer in the chain where it eats snails.
Secondary consumer when eating berries and tertiary consumer when eating snails, since the shrub is the first consumer.
mcqs.specStatementText: Trophic levels are positions, not types of feeder
mcqs.explain: Trophic level is a position in a particular food chain. In shrub → blackbird the bird feeds on the producer and is a primary consumer; in shrub → snail → blackbird it feeds on a primary consumer and is a secondary consumer. Many organisms have a varied diet and occupy different trophic levels in different food chains.
rationales: A student who believes trophic level is a fixed property of a species picks this. The blackbird's level depends on which food chain is being considered; when it eats berries it is a primary consumer.

A student who treats 'secondary consumer' as a synonym for 'carnivore' picks this. Trophic level is set by position in the chain, not by the type of animal; eating berries makes the blackbird a primary consumer in that chain.

Trophic level is a position in a particular food chain. In shrub → blackbird the bird feeds on the producer and is a primary consumer; in shrub → snail → blackbird it feeds on a primary consumer and is a secondary consumer. Many organisms have a varied diet and occupy different trophic levels in different food chains.

A student who counts the producer as the first consumer picks this. Producers are not consumers; the herbivore feeding on the shrub is the primary consumer, so the numbering starts one level lower than this option assumes.

mcqs.q: In a classic study of the Silver Springs ecosystem in Florida, the energy flow through each trophic level (all in kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹) was: producers 20 810; primary consumers 3368; secondary consumers 383; tertiary consumers 21. What percentage of the energy at the primary consumer level was transferred to the secondary consumers?
options: About 1.8%
Exactly 10%
Close to 89%
About 11%
mcqs.specStatementText: Energy pyramids show flow, not stock
mcqs.explain: Transfer between adjacent levels is the energy at the higher level divided by the energy at the level below: 383 ÷ 3368 × 100 = 11.4%, about 11%. An energy pyramid built from these data would show this loss as a large narrowing between the second and third bars.
rationales: A student who compares every level with the producers picks this: 383 ÷ 20 810 × 100 = 1.8%. That is the fraction of the producer energy reaching secondary consumers, not the transfer from primary to secondary consumers.
A student who applies the 10% rule instead of calculating from the data picks this. The rule is only a rough generalization; the measured transfer at this step is 383 ÷ 3368, which is 11.4%.
A student who subtracts and finds the proportion lost picks this: (3368 − 383) ÷ 3368 × 100 = 88.6%. The question asks for the percentage transferred, which is the remaining 11.4%.

Transfer between adjacent levels is the energy at the higher level divided by the energy at the level below: 383 ÷ 3368 × 100 = 11.4%, about 11%. An energy pyramid built from these data would show this loss as a large narrowing between the second and third bars.

mcqs.q: Why is much less energy available to the secondary consumers in a food chain than to the primary consumers?
options: Not all primary consumers are eaten, not all of what is eaten is absorbed, and most absorbed energy is released as heat in respiration.
Primary consumers use up most of their energy in moving and feeding, so that energy is destroyed and no longer exists.
Decomposers, which form the final trophic level, take the energy from primary consumers and return it to the producers.
Respiration in primary consumers captures all the released energy in ATP, and this ATP cannot be passed on to a predator.
mcqs.specStatementText: Most energy is lost at each step
mcqs.explain: Large energy losses occur between trophic levels: uneaten organisms and their dead parts go to decomposers, undigested material is egested as faeces, and most of the energy that is absorbed is released by cell respiration and lost as heat. Only energy in new biomass can pass on.
rationales: Large energy losses occur between trophic levels: uneaten organisms and their dead parts go to decomposers, undigested material is egested as faeces, and most of the energy that is absorbed is released by cell respiration and lost as heat. Only energy in new biomass can pass on.
A student who thinks energy is consumed and disappears picks this. Energy is never destroyed; the energy used for movement is converted to heat by cell respiration and leaves the ecosystem as heat.
A student who places decomposers at the end of the chain and believes they recycle energy picks this. Decomposers release the energy in dead matter as heat; no energy is returned to producers.

A student who thinks respiration is 100% efficient picks this. Energy is lost as heat both when ATP is made and when it is used, and the losses also include uneaten material and faeces; ATP is not what passes between levels in any case.

mcqs.q: A caterpillar ingests leaf material containing 100 kJ of energy. It egests 50 kJ in faeces, releases 35 kJ as heat through cell respiration and stores 15 kJ in new biomass. What happens to the energy in the faeces?
options: It is returned to the plant through the soil, so that the plant can use it again for growth instead of needing sunlight.
It passes to decomposers and detritus feeders, which release it as heat in respiration, not to the next trophic level.
There is no usable energy in the faeces, because the 50 kJ was already released as heat inside the caterpillar's gut.
It has been used up by the caterpillar and ceases to exist, since energy that is not stored as biomass is destroyed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Most energy is lost at each step
mcqs.explain: Decomposers and detritus feeders are not usually considered part of the food chain, but they play a role in its energy transformations: the carbon compounds in faeces are their energy supply, and they oxidize them in cell respiration, releasing the energy as heat. Only the 15 kJ in biomass is available to a bird that eats the caterpillar.
rationales: A student who believes energy is recycled like matter picks this. Decomposers return the elements in faeces to the soil, but the chemical energy is released as heat; the plant obtains its energy only from light.

Decomposers and detritus feeders are not usually considered part of the food chain, but they play a role in its energy transformations: the carbon compounds in faeces are their energy supply, and they oxidize them in cell respiration, releasing the energy as heat. Only the 15 kJ in biomass is available to a bird that eats the caterpillar.

A student who thinks faeces are energy-free waste picks this. Egested material was never absorbed, so its carbon compounds and their 50 kJ are intact; the only heat released by the caterpillar was the 35 kJ from respiration.
A student who believes energy can be destroyed picks this. Energy is conserved; the 50 kJ remains in the carbon compounds of the faeces until decomposers and detritus feeders respire them.

mcqs.q: Why do plants, as well as animals, lose heat to their environment?
options: They do not: heat is produced only by warm-blooded animals; plants merely lose heat that they absorbed from sunlight.
Plants respire only at night, so the heat they lose is produced in darkness and simply builds up until the next day.
Cell respiration in every organism converts some chemical energy to heat, both when ATP is produced and when ATP is used.
Heat is released only when ATP is used in the cell, because the production of ATP in respiration transfers energy with no loss.
mcqs.specStatementText: All organisms leak heat, making and using ATP
mcqs.explain: Heat loss to the environment occurs in both autotrophs and heterotrophs because energy transfers are not 100% efficient: heat is produced when ATP is made in cell respiration and again when the ATP is used in cells.
rationales: A student who links heat production to being warm-blooded picks this. Plants respire continuously and convert chemical energy to heat; a compost heap or a germinating seed pile warms up for exactly this reason.
A student who thinks plants alternate between photosynthesis and respiration picks this. Plants respire at all times, so heat is produced and lost continuously.

Heat loss to the environment occurs in both autotrophs and heterotrophs because energy transfers are not 100% efficient: heat is produced when ATP is made in cell respiration and again when the ATP is used in cells.

A student who assumes respiration captures all the energy in ATP picks this. Energy transfers are not 100% efficient at either stage; heat is produced during ATP production as well as when ATP is used.

mcqs.q: Food chains in most ecosystems have no more than four or five trophic levels. What is the reason for this restriction?
options: The number of trophic levels is set by the number of species in the community, and few communities have more than five.
The tissues of organisms higher in the chain contain less energy per gram, so a predator cannot gain enough energy from each meal.
Decomposers occupy the last trophic level of every chain and take the remaining energy, so no further consumers can be added.
So much energy is lost at each transfer that after a few levels too little remains to support a viable consumer population.
mcqs.specStatementText: Energy losses cap food chains at four or five levels
mcqs.explain: Restrictions on the number of trophic levels are due to energy losses. Most of the energy at each level is lost as heat or passes to decomposers, so at each successive stage there are fewer or smaller organisms and less biomass, and eventually there is not enough energy to sustain another level.
rationales: A student who counts species rather than energy picks this. A rainforest with thousands of species still has food chains of only four or five levels, because energy, not species number, is the limit.
A student who thinks biomass becomes less energy-rich up the chain picks this. Energy content per unit mass is not reduced at higher levels; there is simply less biomass in total.

A student who places decomposers as a top trophic level picks this. Decomposers are not part of food chains and receive dead matter from every level; the limit comes from cumulative energy losses at each transfer.

Restrictions on the number of trophic levels are due to energy losses. Most of the energy at each level is lost as heat or passes to decomposers, so at each successive stage there are fewer or smaller organisms and less biomass, and eventually there is not enough energy to sustain another level.

mcqs.q: In a model grassland ecosystem the dry biomass per square metre is: producers 800 g, primary consumers 100 g, secondary consumers 15 g, tertiary consumers 2 g. Samples of dry biomass from each level release similar amounts of energy per gram when burned. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Energy per unit mass is similar at every level, so the fall in energy available up the chain is due to the fall in biomass.
The biomass at higher levels must be poorer in energy per gram, since energy falls even faster than mass along the chain.
The data show that producers accumulate 800 g of biomass per square metre each year, which is their primary production.
The data confirm that exactly 10% of biomass is transferred between each pair of trophic levels in this ecosystem.
mcqs.specStatementText: Energy losses cap food chains at four or five levels
mcqs.explain: At each successive stage there are fewer organisms or smaller organisms, so there is less biomass, but the energy content per unit mass is not reduced. The burning data confirm the second point, so the reduced energy at higher levels must come from the smaller quantity of biomass.
rationales: At each successive stage there are fewer organisms or smaller organisms, so there is less biomass, but the energy content per unit mass is not reduced. The burning data confirm the second point, so the reduced energy at higher levels must come from the smaller quantity of biomass.

A student who expects tissue to become less energy-rich up the chain picks this. The burning results contradict it: each gram of biomass releases a similar amount of energy whatever its trophic level.

A student who confuses a stock with a rate picks this. The figures are the biomass present at one time (g m⁻²); primary production is a rate of accumulation (g m⁻² yr⁻¹) and cannot be read from a snapshot.
A student who reaches for the 10% rule without checking picks this. The ratios here are 12.5%, 15% and 13%, and in any case a biomass snapshot does not measure transfer of energy over time.

mcqs.q: Which are the correct units for primary production?
options: Grams of carbon per square metre of land
Grams of carbon per square metre per year
Kilojoules per square metre per year
Grams of carbon per individual per year
mcqs.specStatementText: Primary production is a rate of carbon accumulation
mcqs.explain: Primary production is the accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs. It is a rate, so the units are mass of carbon per unit area per unit time, usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹.
rationales: A student who equates production with the biomass present picks this. Grams per square metre measure a stock of biomass at one time; production must include per unit time because it is a rate of accumulation.
Primary production is the accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs. It is a rate, so the units are mass of carbon per unit area per unit time, usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹.

A student who carries over the units of an energy pyramid picks this. Energy flow is expressed in kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹, but primary production is defined by the mass of carbon accumulated, so its units are g m⁻² yr⁻¹.
A student who thinks of production as the growth of an individual plant picks this. Production is a property of an area of ecosystem, measured per square metre, so that biomes can be compared.

mcqs.q: A widely cited compilation of net primary production (g of dry biomass m⁻² yr⁻¹) gives typical values of about 2200 for tropical rainforest, 600 for temperate grassland, 125 for open ocean and 90 for desert. What do these data show?
options: The desert value must be an error, because deserts receive the most sunlight and primary production depends on light alone.
Rainforest has the highest value simply because it contains the most standing biomass, not because it grows faster.
Biomes differ greatly in capacity to accumulate biomass; deserts have high light but water limits their photosynthesis.
Rainforest soils are richer in carbon compounds, which the trees absorb through their roots to build biomass faster.
mcqs.specStatementText: Primary production is a rate of carbon accumulation
mcqs.explain: Biomes vary in their capacity to accumulate biomass. Photosynthesis and growth need water, warmth and mineral nutrients as well as light, so a hot desert, despite intense sunlight, has a production more than twenty times lower than a rainforest.
rationales: A student who treats light as the only factor picks this. Light is necessary but not sufficient; without water, stomata close and photosynthesis stops, so desert production is genuinely very low.

A student who confuses biomass with production picks this. The figures are rates of accumulation per year; a rainforest genuinely fixes and retains far more carbon per square metre each year than the other biomes.

Biomes vary in their capacity to accumulate biomass. Photosynthesis and growth need water, warmth and mineral nutrients as well as light, so a hot desert, despite intense sunlight, has a production more than twenty times lower than a rainforest.

A student who believes plants take carbon from the soil picks this. The carbon in new biomass comes from atmospheric carbon dioxide fixed in photosynthesis; roots absorb water and mineral ions, not carbon compounds.

mcqs.q: In every ecosystem, secondary production is lower than primary production. What is the reason for this?
options: Everything a heterotroph absorbs becomes biomass, so secondary production is lower only because heterotrophs eat relatively little.
The biomass of heterotrophs contains less energy per gram than plant biomass, so less carbon is stored in each gram.
Autotrophs do not lose biomass by cell respiration, whereas heterotrophs do, so only heterotrophs suffer this loss.
Heterotrophs convert much of the carbon they consume to carbon dioxide and water in cell respiration, so less becomes biomass.
mcqs.specStatementText: Secondary production is lower than primary
mcqs.explain: Secondary production is the accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by heterotrophs. Due to loss of biomass when carbon compounds are converted to carbon dioxide and water in cell respiration, secondary production is lower than primary production in an ecosystem.
rationales: A student who thinks assimilation is complete picks this. Much of the absorbed carbon is respired to carbon dioxide and water and never becomes biomass; that respiratory loss, not a small appetite, is the reason.
A student who thinks animal tissue is poorer in energy picks this. Energy content per unit mass is not reduced at higher trophic levels; the difference is in the quantity of biomass accumulated.

A student who thinks plants do not respire picks this. Autotrophs also respire and lose carbon as carbon dioxide; secondary production is lower because heterotrophs start from the smaller pool of carbon that reaches them and then respire much of it.

Secondary production is the accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by heterotrophs. Due to loss of biomass when carbon compounds are converted to carbon dioxide and water in cell respiration, secondary production is lower than primary production in an ecosystem.

mcqs.q: A student draws a carbon cycle diagram for a pond. Which set of labelled arrows is correct?
options: Photosynthesis: CO₂ → producers; feeding: producers → consumers; respiration: producers, consumers, decomposers → CO₂.
Photosynthesis: CO₂ → producers; feeding: producers → consumers; decomposition of dead organisms → CO₂, with no other return.
Absorption: soil carbon → producers; feeding: producers → consumers; respiration: all organisms → CO₂ in the air and water.
Photosynthesis: CO₂ → producers; feeding: producers → consumers; respiration: consumers and decomposers only → CO₂ in the air.
mcqs.specStatementText: Drawing the carbon cycle
mcqs.explain: Carbon is recycled in ecosystems by photosynthesis, feeding and respiration. Photosynthesis fixes carbon dioxide into the carbon compounds of producers, feeding passes carbon compounds along food chains, and cell respiration in all organisms, including the producers and the decomposers, returns carbon dioxide.
rationales: Carbon is recycled in ecosystems by photosynthesis, feeding and respiration. Photosynthesis fixes carbon dioxide into the carbon compounds of producers, feeding passes carbon compounds along food chains, and cell respiration in all organisms, including the producers and the decomposers, returns carbon dioxide.

A student who thinks carbon leaves organisms only after death picks this. Living producers and consumers release carbon dioxide continuously by cell respiration; decay is only the route for carbon remaining in dead matter.
A student who believes plants take carbon from the soil picks this. Producers obtain carbon by fixing carbon dioxide in photosynthesis; the arrow into producers must start from carbon dioxide.
A student who thinks plants photosynthesize instead of respiring picks this. Producers respire as well, so a respiration arrow must also run from producers to carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Suppose measurements in a forest over one year give: carbon fixed by photosynthesis 1200 g m⁻²; carbon released by plant respiration 600 g m⁻²; carbon released by the respiration of animals, fungi and bacteria 650 g m⁻². Is the forest a carbon sink or a carbon source in that year?
options: A carbon sink, with a net uptake of 550 g m⁻², because only heterotroph respiration returns carbon to the atmosphere.
A carbon source, with a net release of 50 g m⁻², because total respiration (1250) exceeds photosynthesis (1200).
A carbon sink, because a forest full of photosynthesizing trees removes carbon dioxide no matter what its respiration is.
Neither, because an ecosystem recycles its carbon internally and has no net exchange with the atmosphere.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sink or source depends on photosynthesis versus respiration
mcqs.explain: If respiration exceeds photosynthesis there is a net release of carbon dioxide. Respiration here includes all organisms: 600 + 650 = 1250 g m⁻², which is 50 g m⁻² more than the 1200 g m⁻² fixed, so the forest was a source that year.
rationales: A student who leaves out plant respiration picks this: 1200 − 650 = 550. Plants respire too, releasing 600 g m⁻² here, so the true balance is 1200 − 1250 = −50 g m⁻².

If respiration exceeds photosynthesis there is a net release of carbon dioxide. Respiration here includes all organisms: 600 + 650 = 1250 g m⁻², which is 50 g m⁻² more than the 1200 g m⁻² fixed, so the forest was a source that year.

A student who assumes vegetation always makes an ecosystem a sink picks this. Sink or source depends on the balance between photosynthesis and total respiration, and in this year respiration was greater.
A student who treats the ecosystem as a closed system picks this. Ecosystems are open: carbon dioxide crosses the boundary in both directions, and here the outflow exceeded the inflow by 50 g m⁻².

mcqs.q: Which statement about the combustion of biomass, peat, coal, oil and natural gas is correct?
options: All formed from organisms at about the same time in the distant past, so burning any of them has the same significance for the carbon cycle.
Burning biomass such as wood releases no carbon dioxide because it is renewable, whereas burning the fossil fuels does release it.
All release carbon dioxide that was originally fixed by photosynthesis, at dates ranging from recent years to hundreds of millions of years ago.
Coal, oil and natural gas release carbon of mineral origin that did not come from living organisms, unlike biomass and peat.
mcqs.specStatementText: Burning returns fixed carbon to the air
mcqs.explain: Combustion of each of these releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. They vary in date of formation: biomass may be a few years old, peat accumulates over thousands of years, and coal, oil and natural gas formed over tens to hundreds of millions of years, but all began as carbon fixed by autotrophs.
rationales: A student who treats all fuels of organic origin as one category picks this. Their dates of formation differ enormously, from living biomass to coal hundreds of millions of years old, and this affects how long the carbon had been out of circulation.

A student who reads 'carbon-neutral' as 'no carbon dioxide' picks this. Combustion of biomass releases carbon dioxide just as fossil fuels do; the difference is only that regrowth may fix an equivalent amount later.

Combustion of each of these releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. They vary in date of formation: biomass may be a few years old, peat accumulates over thousands of years, and coal, oil and natural gas formed over tens to hundreds of millions of years, but all began as carbon fixed by autotrophs.
A student who thinks 'fossil fuel' means a mineral picks this. Coal, oil and gas formed from the remains of organisms, so their carbon was fixed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis long ago.

mcqs.q: Three events release carbon dioxide: a lightning strike ignites a dry grassland; a farmer burns crop stubble after harvest; a power station burns coal. Which comparison is correct?
options: Only the coal releases carbon dioxide, because the grass and the stubble are renewable biomass and so are carbon-neutral fuels.
The carbon in the coal and the carbon in the stubble were both fixed at about the same time, so the three releases are all equivalent.
The coal releases carbon dioxide of geological origin that was not fixed by photosynthesis, unlike the grass and the crop stubble.
All three are combustion releasing carbon dioxide; the first is natural, but human activity has greatly increased combustion rates.
mcqs.specStatementText: Burning returns fixed carbon to the air
mcqs.explain: Combustion following lightning strikes sometimes happens naturally, but human activities such as burning crop residues and fossil fuels have greatly increased combustion rates. In each case carbon compounds are oxidized and carbon dioxide is released to the atmosphere.
rationales: A student who equates renewable with carbon-free picks this. Burning grass and stubble releases carbon dioxide immediately; carbon-neutrality refers only to possible later regrowth.

A student who thinks all combustible carbon stores are the same age picks this. The stubble's carbon was fixed within the last year; the coal's was fixed hundreds of millions of years ago and had been locked out of the atmosphere ever since.
A student who regards coal as a mineral picks this. Coal formed from plant remains, so its carbon was fixed by photosynthesis in the distant past.

Combustion following lightning strikes sometimes happens naturally, but human activities such as burning crop residues and fossil fuels have greatly increased combustion rates. In each case carbon compounds are oxidized and carbon dioxide is released to the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: At Mauna Loa, atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration rises to a peak each May and falls to a minimum each September or October, a swing of several parts per million. What causes this annual fluctuation?
options: In the Northern Hemisphere growing season photosynthesis exceeds respiration, drawing carbon dioxide down; in autumn and winter respiration exceeds photosynthesis.
People burn more fuel for heating in the Northern Hemisphere winter, so combustion raises carbon dioxide until spring and it falls again in summer.
Plants respire only in winter, when they cannot photosynthesize, so carbon dioxide is released only in the cold months and absorbed in the warm months.
Biological processes are too small to change the whole atmosphere, so the regular swing must be an artefact of the measuring instruments at the observatory.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading the Keeling Curve
mcqs.explain: The annual fluctuation is analysed in terms of photosynthesis and respiration. Most land, and so most vegetation, is in the Northern Hemisphere; from May to September net uptake by photosynthesis lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide, and from autumn to spring respiration and decomposition return it.
rationales: The annual fluctuation is analysed in terms of photosynthesis and respiration. Most land, and so most vegetation, is in the Northern Hemisphere; from May to September net uptake by photosynthesis lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide, and from autumn to spring respiration and decomposition return it.

A student who attributes every feature of the curve to fuel burning picks this. Seasonal changes in combustion are small compared with the seasonal swing in photosynthesis; combustion explains the long-term trend, not the annual cycle.
A student who sees photosynthesis and respiration as alternatives picks this. Plants respire all year round; in summer photosynthesis simply exceeds respiration, and in winter the balance reverses.

A student with no sense of the scale of global fluxes picks this. The yearly exchange of carbon dioxide between organisms and the atmosphere is huge, easily large enough to produce the measured swing, which is confirmed at many stations worldwide.

mcqs.q: The annual mean carbon dioxide concentration at Mauna Loa was about 317 ppm in 1960 and about 414 ppm in 2020. What is the accepted explanation for this long-term trend?
options: Breathing by the growing human population, together with its livestock, has added more carbon dioxide each year than plants can absorb.
Combustion of fossil fuels and biomass releases carbon fixed long ago faster than photosynthesis and other processes remove it.
Increased volcanic activity has released carbon dioxide from deep within the Earth, and this geological source dominates the trend.
Fossil fuels release mineral carbon that was not part of the carbon cycle, so it accumulates because organisms are unable to take it up.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading the Keeling Curve
mcqs.explain: The long-term trend is analysed in terms of combustion. Burning coal, oil, gas and biomass adds carbon dioxide that had been locked out of the atmosphere, at a rate exceeding the net uptake by ecosystems and oceans, so the concentration climbs by an average of about 1.6 ppm per year over this period.
rationales: A student who combines 'respiration releases carbon dioxide' with population growth picks this. The carbon exhaled by people and livestock was fixed from the atmosphere by crops within recent years, so it returns carbon already in circulation rather than adding to the total.

The long-term trend is analysed in terms of combustion. Burning coal, oil, gas and biomass adds carbon dioxide that had been locked out of the atmosphere, at a rate exceeding the net uptake by ecosystems and oceans, so the concentration climbs by an average of about 1.6 ppm per year over this period.

A student who thinks volcanoes are the main source of atmospheric carbon dioxide picks this. Volcanic emissions are a tiny fraction of those from combustion of fossil fuels, and there has been no sustained rise in volcanic activity since 1960.

A student who regards fossil carbon as non-biological picks this. Fossil-fuel carbon was fixed by photosynthesis and is chemically identical to any other carbon dioxide; it accumulates because it is being added faster than photosynthesis and ocean uptake remove it, not because it cannot be absorbed.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the recycling of chemical elements in ecosystems is correct?
options: Only carbon is recycled; the other elements are absorbed from the soil, used by organisms and then used up, so they must be replaced.
Elements are released from dead organisms automatically as they die, so decomposers play only a minor part in recycling them.
Both the chemical elements and the energy in dead organisms are recycled by decomposers and returned to producers for reuse.
All elements required by organisms are recycled; decomposers release them from dead matter in forms that autotrophs can take up.
mcqs.specStatementText: Every element is recycled, and decomposers make it happen
mcqs.explain: All elements used by living organisms, not just carbon, are recycled in ecosystems, and decomposers play a key role by breaking down the carbon compounds of dead organic matter and returning the elements to the abiotic environment as simple inorganic substances.
rationales: A student who has studied only the carbon cycle picks this. Elements are not used up; nitrogen, phosphorus and every other element required by organisms pass repeatedly between organisms and the environment.

A student who sees death and decay as the same event picks this. The elements in a dead organism are locked in complex carbon compounds until decomposers digest them; without decomposers, recycling would largely stop.
A student who believes energy cycles like matter picks this. Decomposers return elements to the environment, but they release the energy in dead matter as heat, which producers cannot use.

All elements used by living organisms, not just carbon, are recycled in ecosystems, and decomposers play a key role by breaking down the carbon compounds of dead organic matter and returning the elements to the abiotic environment as simple inorganic substances.

mcqs.q: A farmer harvests and sells the whole crop from a field every year and returns no plant material or manure. Soil analysis shows that the mineral nutrients available to plants decline year on year. Which explanation is correct?
options: The elements built into crop biomass are removed from the field instead of being returned by decomposers, so the cycle is broken.
Mineral elements are used up and destroyed by the growing plants, so any field loses them whether or not the crop is removed.
The crop absorbed carbon compounds from the soil to build up its biomass, and it is this carbon that the soil is running short of.
Decomposers in the soil cannot produce new mineral ions fast enough to keep pace with the amount that the crop plants absorb each year.
mcqs.specStatementText: Every element is recycled, and decomposers make it happen
mcqs.explain: In a natural ecosystem the elements in plant biomass return to the soil when decomposers break down dead matter and faeces. Exporting the whole crop removes those elements from the ecosystem each year, so the recycling that would normally replenish the soil cannot occur.
rationales: In a natural ecosystem the elements in plant biomass return to the soil when decomposers break down dead matter and faeces. Exporting the whole crop removes those elements from the ecosystem each year, so the recycling that would normally replenish the soil cannot occur.
A student who thinks elements are consumed picks this. Elements are never destroyed; the ones in this field are lost only because they leave in the harvested biomass rather than being recycled.

A student who believes plants feed on soil carbon picks this. The crop's carbon came from atmospheric carbon dioxide; what the soil loses are the mineral elements, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, that were built into the exported biomass.

A student who thinks decomposers manufacture nutrients picks this. Decomposers only release elements already present in dead organic matter; if that matter is removed from the field, there is nothing for them to recycle.

mcqs.q: In the Silver Springs study the energy flow through the trophic levels (kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹) was: producers 20 810; primary consumers 3368; secondary consumers 383; tertiary consumers 21. Which statement about an energy pyramid constructed from these data is correct?
options: The bars represent the energy stored in the organisms present at each level when sampled, so the units should be kcal m⁻² with no time component.
Four horizontal bars with producers at the base, each bar's width proportional to the energy flowing through that level per unit area per unit time.
A fifth bar for decomposers should be drawn at the top, because they form the final trophic level and receive the remaining 21 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.
The bars narrow because the tissues at each higher level contain less energy per gram, so the widths show energy per unit mass of biomass.
mcqs.specStatementText: Energy pyramids show flow, not stock
mcqs.explain: An energy pyramid is constructed from research data for a specific ecosystem: one bar per trophic level, producers at the base, widths proportional to energy flow in kcal (or kJ) m⁻² yr⁻¹, so the narrowing between bars represents the energy losses between levels.
rationales: A student who treats an energy pyramid as a snapshot like a pyramid of biomass picks this. Each bar is a rate of energy flow through the level, which is why the units include per year.

An energy pyramid is constructed from research data for a specific ecosystem: one bar per trophic level, producers at the base, widths proportional to energy flow in kcal (or kJ) m⁻² yr⁻¹, so the narrowing between bars represents the energy losses between levels.

A student who places decomposers as the last trophic level picks this. Decomposers are not usually considered part of food chains; they receive dead matter and faeces from every level and are not a bar in the pyramid.

A student who thinks biomass becomes poorer in energy up the chain picks this. Energy content per unit mass is not reduced; the bars narrow because less total energy flows through each successive level.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C4.2 Transfers of energy and matter

specStatements.text: Ecosystems are open: energy and matter both cross the boundary
Sunlight powers almost every ecosystem, and laws describe rather than explain
Chemical energy passes along the chain by feeding
Drawing food chains and webs
Decomposers live on dead organic matter
Autotrophs build carbon compounds from inorganic ones, using outside energy
Light for photoautotrophs, oxidation reactions for chemoautotrophs
Heterotrophs digest, absorb and rebuild
Every organism respires, all the time
Trophic levels are positions, not types of feeder
Energy pyramids show flow, not stock
Most energy is lost at each step
All organisms leak heat, making and using ATP
Energy losses cap food chains at four or five levels
Primary production is a rate of carbon accumulation
Secondary production is lower than primary
Drawing the carbon cycle
Sink or source depends on photosynthesis versus respiration
Burning returns fixed carbon to the air
Reading the Keeling Curve
Respiration and photosynthesis feed each other's gases
Every element is recycled, and decomposers make it happen

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nutrition is classified only as photoautotrophic, chemoautotrophic and heterotrophic. No concept, misconception or item names photoheterotrophs or asks students to distinguish organisms that use light for energy but obtain carbon from other organisms.

Recycling of elements other than carbon is tested only as the general principle that all elements are recycled and that decomposers play a key role. Nitrogen and phosphorus are named only as examples of elements that are recycled; no nitrogen-cycle processes, organisms or compounds (nitrification, nitrogen fixation, denitrification, nitrate, ammonium) are named or tested.

No food chain or trophic-level item places decomposers or detritus feeders at a trophic level; they appear only in their stated role in energy transformations, receiving energy from dead matter and faeces of every level and releasing it as heat. The belief that they form a final trophic level is treated as a misconception.
